January the 25th. Was there a particular time? Was it in the country? In the country, yeah. I fought on the rice farm there. Still on it. And I came up on the rice farm. And I was a man who played the violins at the end of eight years. I was bringing my music for it when I was eager to work. And I started playing professional around New Orleans, ballrooms, and parks, street parades, drums. And I played with a little brass band around a place called Jamestown in Louisiana, what they call the Beehive Brass Band. And I played a few engagements on drums with Professor Claiborne William of Donnisonville, St. Joseph Band at that time. Then I played around New Orleans up until about around 1940. Then I left Chicago, Illinois. And in Chicago, Illinois, I joined the original three-hole band. That was called the Olympia Band in New Orleans. George Backlade, Freddie Keppert, Roy Palmer, Tubby Hall, and myself on the bass. I studied bass based on Professor Jackson in Chicago. Then I studied trombone in the meantime because that was always my favorite instrument. And my inspiration in the trombone were kid-roy. So I copied that style fully good. And the boys used to call me young-roy around Chicago. So around 1990, my lips went bad. So I just stuck to the spring bass and I made better success out of it. And everyone thought that I did such a wonderful job. And in my bass career, I always admired William Moran and Kimberl, New Orleans. A very fine bass player at that time. So I copied what they were putting down in the line of tone. And fingering, you see the bass violin is a chord instrument, like any other instrument that's supposed to be called. But going back to the bass players of the day, well, I can see a fellow like Milton Hilt, who's very, very fine artist. Slam still, very fine. Jimmy Blanton, one of the greatest solos of all time. And the average bass player, though, they play more like they play in the drum. They play on one string all night. Four in the bow and everything. Never a chord. So I can tell you that a bass is a very fine instrument that's playing right. And I still like to play the bass. And I think I can do a very good job on the bass today. Perhaps I might not be as fast as I used to be, but I don't know. All I have to do is be around somebody that can play because I'm very sensitive about playing. As long as I'm with a band out that can play, I can play. And I really, I had a year with Kidd over his band and I really enjoyed it because he's one fellow that I always liked his playing, who liked to play in his band, always admired him. And so I had the opportunity of playing here in Gabriel. And that was to the height of my ambition. And I really enjoyed it. And I made quite a few platters with him. And I think it was very good. And I thought that was very good myself. And I also liked some dates that he made after Calvin Alcon, close to Walker B. And Maple Leaf Rag, I thought that was very, very fun. Well, Roy Palmer, that was Lewis, I mean, Lawrence Doey's band. Lil Hardin Armstrong on the piano, and Lawrence Doey on the clarinet, Sidney Bache clarinet, Bab Frank piccolo, and Sugar Johnny, cornet, and Toby Halls on the drum. That was a very fine organization, very, very good.

Well, he was very fine, very outstanding piccolo player.

Oh, no. He played fiddle parts on the piccolo. And he was a very fine piccolo player, because I can tell from some people that I met in the Georgia Ministrel Brass Band. He was once a member of that. Well, we call him Papa Teal here. That was Lorenzo Teal's father. He played clarinet in the band. And also, old man, Piku. He was a clarinet player in the Georgia Ministrel Band. That's way before my time, but I can remember fellas that just tell me, like, Fred Simpson, he was the leader of the band of New York. And he told me that those guys played with him. And they were very fine.
And Bab Frank read?
Or Bab Frank could read anything that was for the piccolo to read, and he played the fiddle parts on the piccolo.

Well, he could play any. You know what I mean? That makes a good musician. Myself, I studied the bass and trombone. I can play what I have to play my part, and I can fake as well. So that makes the best man. That's what they're looking for. A man can fake and read. You see, a man that can fake and read, he can get a job quicker, because he can better use it. A lot of times, you don't have time to look at music or turn over music. See what I mean? Duke Elliman Band, we made a rehearsal once, and we played the number down a couple of times, and after that, we could do a little more than just looking at the arrangement, because you had to be a little more than a musician. And otherwise, you could use a man that improvised. See what I mean? My success in the music game, I didn't stay up there just playing bass notes. I used it for a guy, you know? I played a voice note in every bar. Then I run my changes. It's coming from a man that knows the instrument, and he can run his changes. All you have to do is know the instrument, then you know what you're doing. You can control it. See what I mean? Yeah. Some, you meet a lot of good musicians, but they're just technical. They're just technical. It's no kind of lift. Understand? Yeah. And so that makes the great artists. Well, and otherwise, we, in the Orleans, we call it soul. That's all. We call it soul. I have a very dear friend of mine. He's from New Orleans, Sidney Bashir. He doesn't read at all. That's right.
I know Sidney Bashir.
But he can play from the Grand Opera down.
That's right.

I was playing at the Mantis in 1917. James P. Europe from New York came then with his band, the 15th. That was one of the, at that time, they were one of the finest military bands I ever heard. And he had 12 clarinet players. So he came in the ducks and he listened to Sidney. So he called Sidney over to the table, him and Noble Sisson of New York. And he asked Sidney to join his band. Would he join his band? Can Sidney join his band? He said, well, Mr. Europe, he said, I don't read. He said, I'd like for you to come to my rehearsal down at the Carla Sims. And so he accepted the engagement. So he asked me, he says, bro, come on down to me. I'm going to hear the 15th band. I said, you might enjoy that. So I said, yeah, okay. So we went on down. He did. At that time, they played, uh, Fortin Pleasant. So, he listened. So Mr. Europe asked him would he like to sit in after hearing his concert numbers. So he said, yes, I'll sit in. And he sat in. And there's a clarinet cadenza in closing plastic. And when that guy got through playing the cadenza, well, uh, Jim Europe 12 clarinet players couldn't come on. Because they hadn't heard anything. That's what I tell you about soul. The man got soul. He got the feeling and the phrase and everything that goes. You know what I mean? He's a real artist. And he's like myself. He's very sensitive. If something isn't going wrong, I'm in a section, a rhythm section, if something going wrong, it'll drag me. You know what I mean? You got to drag me. Because you've been used to hearing one beat and you hear something else. You know, if you take the piano players today or the drummers of today, they're coming up with what they call bop and progression. Well, that doesn't fit in Dixieland at all. It tears you up. And I had the opportunity to run them kind of fellas that said they was a piano player, but they never played chord. See what I mean? Everything was bop. Well, it doesn't make sense in a Dixieland band because you're a customer of hearing chords. Well, we'll go back to Ellington band, fuller chords. Fuller chords and rhythm. Ellington band, if the saxophone players had what we call a lick chorus, the brass wasn't sitting down there, as we call them in New Orleans soldier, soldier in the band. They play a lot of rhythm. And if the brass had a lick chorus, well, the saxophone would play rhythm. You know what I mean? The feeling. You know what I mean? Rhythm. But the man didn't write that, of course not. He didn't have that written, but it just comes from soul. You take fellas like Barney Bigger, Johnny Hodges, Arthur Hardrick, they're great. Conny.
Did Ellington write much of that out at all? So when we say like black and tan fantasy, when you make that up?

Well, it comes from improvising. Black and tan fantasy had a score to it, but he had thought that the organization had so many great men in it, they could improvise. And they could put in things that would make Mr. Ellington smile and everybody else, because it was out the ordinary. And the first big band had individuals to get up and play something. What they do in the day was nothing, isn't anything new to Duke Ellington's original orchestra. He had men like Bubba Miley in the small band, and he had men like Tricky Sand. He had men like Bigger in the small band.
One time Barney told me something about how you all took the tune, that was one of Oliver's numbers, I think, in the Camp Meeting Blues. And you were part of that bar, the Creole Love.

Yeah, Creole Love called, and we also, high number we had written by Lorenzo Teal, Mood Enigo. Oh, was that really? Oh, yeah, that was really. But you see, the Ellington is a doctor of music, I'll call him, because he can make a tune a little better and sound a little better than what it is. It'll come from his brain, it still comes from the same thing of improvising. Now, I see in places, I take an eighth note, if it's on the score, and I can make a thirty-second note out of it, but I know where to put it at. Now, if I were playing an arrangement like Rhapsody Blues or a concert number, I could only play it the way the score is, because there wasn't no place to improvise. You know what I mean? Because every note counted in a particular tune of that kind. Now, I had the opportunity of making a picture with the oil cow vanities, the Vanity. And they had a movement in that, for the bass, and the movement of the Hungarian Rhapsody. But only, I rehearsed it down a couple of times, and when I went and rehearsed it a third time, well, we had some dancing girls, the Vanity's chorus. And I see where it was fit that I could swing the second Hungarian Rhapsody movement. And I played it in swing time, and the director thought it was great, and that's what they wanted. But you see, I could tell from the girls dancing, from the taps when they come, when their feet come down, I see where I could build that little girl. See, and that comes from the eyes. The arranger doesn't write that. See what I mean? But after a while, you can sit in the orchestra, and, well, I don't know, I sit just on, besides Elgar's band, that's the only big orchestra. And when I played with Elgar, there wasn't no arrangement, but Duke, the only was the stock arrangement. But Elgin arranges his own music, but then at the same time, he could get a lot of ideas, too, after he would hear a record. And he could get ideas for the bass. And I had men like, I had men like, what's the boy arranged for Tommy Dawson? Cy Alley, huh? To compliment me and told me, Mr. Bro said, I'm very glad to have met you, but we, all of us, learned a lot from your bass and arranged it. Oh. And I think so, because I'm the first man that, that started what we call the walking bass. You see, the walking bass, and I was taught to play bass up and down, you know? Just like a metronome, you know?
In the old days, before you, when you were just a kid and heard the first bass players, how many beats in a major did they play? Did they play something like that? Two beats.

Two beats. Two beats. And more of the bow. The bow is very eccentric in some places. Now, the bass players of today, they don't use a bow. They don't know what it's for. See what I mean? And the bass comes in, plays a very big part on the string bass, in places you can use it. You know what I mean? Yeah. Some places you can use it like anything else, but it's knowing where to use it.
Have you any idea who the first people were that played bass? Who was maybe the first one?

Well, I had them. The first I heard were Billy Murray, Kimball, and Steve Brown, one of the finest, too. I knew him in the front. I'm a Goldcats kitten. Well, he's from New Orleans. Yeah. He played with the Browns Band. He left here with the Browns Band around 1913. And he have a son. I don't know if he's still a player, but he's one of the finest, I heard Steve Brown's son. Steve Brown is now the business agent for the Detroit local.
I met him in Detroit. His brother is still here.

And he's very, very fine. He didn't read anything. But I'm telling you, you couldn't tell a different way that your man just knew. He sat in in the Paul Whiteman Band. He made some of the finest records Paul Whiteman Band made in the bass line. The finest I heard. And a very fine fellow. And he thinks there's nobody in the world like me. Now he thinks I'm the greatest. And I think he's the greatest. See what I mean?
He is.

If you ever hear in his record, you can tell. You see, I, myself, I'm very cranky about the tones. I played whole notes for hours when I was playing that for the tone. That's why I could deliver the tone that I do deliver on the bass. I know I have a good tone on the bass. I might be the best. But anyway, with the bow of the fingers. Because you hear some records, you don't hear a bass. You hear this. You see? You hear a knocking like you're knocking against a bow. Well, that comes from people that didn't study tones. Whole notes is very essential in music because you get the tone in your ear. And also, to make a better tone, the chromatics is very essential. You play chromatics for hours, nothing else. You've got to get the tone in your head. You know what I mean? And then, in the meantime, the artist must have some kind of natural ability, too. You know? You must have some natural ability to be a player of any kind.
I'm going to ask some more about that other first band we were talking about. When you had Bache and Lawrence Dewey both, did they both play clarinet or did Bache use the soprano sound?

No. Bache were playing clarinet at the time. And one of the best clarinet players ever left New Orleans or anybody's place. Because he, still today, I just heard him in Paris and I'm telling you, he's Mr. Paris. But he played the soprano. And right today, he played better clarinet than the average clarinet player. But he devoted his time with the soprano. He took up the soprano in 1918. And he wanted to play soprano. He played anything with a reed on it. He played. And he, the first fellow I heard, made a one band record. I guess you heard it, Mr. Russell.
The chic of Arabian.
The chic Arabian. He played trumpet. He played bass. He played piano. He played drums. He played trombone. And clarinet, himself.
When you used the two clarinets, did they play in harmony? Or did Cape Turnabout have any solos? Or one band record.

He played a plagata to what Lawrence Dewey played. And sometime, he played the top. He played the lead. And he could play a plagata. Well, that comes from natural ability. Man, just real artists. You know what I mean? And for, for singer, well, he's the best in the world. He's the best in the world. And the next best I heard for singer since, including Basset, was Biggar. And, Bonnie Biggar with Louis Armstrong, played more clarinet. Obligata and filling in than anybody I know outside of Sidney Basset. Because he had the soul. And also, Jimmy Newman. Jimmy Newman was an outstanding clarinet. Yeah, I heard that.
Oh, yeah.
The tone of the biggest is room. Very fine. Very fine artists.
Who's this fellow Moran that you mentioned? William Moran.
He's from New Orleans. He had a son by the name of John Moran. Moran, a Moran, a letter. Of course, we always say Moran. Oh, oh. Billy Moran. Billy Moran, yeah. That's him.
And Lawrence is still a player.
And he had a fellow, his son by the name of John Moran. He was a very fine guitar player. Lawrence played fine guitar, too. And his son, Simon Moran. Very fine bass player. I don't know if y'all are.
He's still here. I heard him play one.
Oh, he's very good.
He's still here.
I thought he was dead. I know John is dead.
John was dead. John died in New York.
Yeah, I know he's dead.
Simon was still here last time here. Eddie is. Did Eddie die? There's another man. I didn't know Eddie.
Oh, and they all played.
I didn't know.
They all played bass.
I didn't know. That was a very good one. Oh, one other little point. That was on the record strange. How do you spell your last name?

My last name? I spelled my last name B-R-A-U-D. But the proper way to spell it my name is B-R-E-A-U-X. But Brow was such a large family. I was amongst some of them Sunday. And then some of the bros hadn't never seen me before. seen you before because some of them weren't born. So it looked like the mail would get mixed up. And so we just, my father just changed the last name.
Your father changed the name? The name, the last name. But my name
is Bro, B-R-E-A-U-X. So that's the way all the Bro's spelled. On our family, we were in the same section. And they were all farmers and bricklayers, so they lived all in the same section.
How far up the river is that where you were born?
Oh, that's about 65 miles from there. A little place they call Brookstown, Louisiana.
Is that Aubin moving down around there?
No. Abin. Abin. Yeah, well that's near Donisonville.
When did you move down here then?

Oh, I must have came to New Orleans around 1911. And I stayed in New Orleans. And I lived from New Orleans for Chicago. At that time, I was living on St. Mary's Street between Nunciation and Chippy Wall. Irish Channel, they called it. Yeah. Kind of rough neighborhood.
Yeah, I guess uptown, it was rough someplace.
Yeah. Well, it was strictly Irish neighborhood. They were pretty rough boys. Yeah.
Your first instrument was violin, is that right?
Violin and mandolin. Oh, man. And I played a little guitar. And in 1918, I played on a medicine show, Trombone, in Chicago. That's when I started my first
trombone day. Did you ever play in the district?
No, I was too young to go in the district. I couldn't go in the district when I was 18. You had to be 21.
Yeah. What year were you born?
So, I was wondering, how come you changed to tuba for a while?

Well, I tried. I didn't, I wasn't crazy about the tuba, but there was a few records that they wanted to make on tuba, and I could play tuba. It was very easy for me. And I did a pretty good job. I guess you heard the mooch. I can't give you anything but love. Black and tan? Well, that was tuba. No, no. Black and tan was that big tone from that bass. That's what you heard. That's right. That's the old London band when they first came out. Yeah. Great.
What was that other one that you come through? You said, good on Saturday night.

Well, I went, I went, I went, I went, Copenhagen. No, I went Blackpool in 1933. And I was playing on one side of the hall, and it was an English band playing on another, on the other side of the hall. So, he come in and asked me what kind of tuba did I use. So, I said, there's the tuba right up there, son. He couldn't believe it. He thought, yeah, string bass. Yeah, string bass, see. That's right. What about Saturday Night Function or Double Jack Stomp? Oh, I made all that on the screen. Double Jack Stomp, I wrote that tune. You wrote that tune? Yeah. How'd you get that name? Well, from Amos Nandy. Yeah. Amos Nandy was in Raid that time, so Eldon got that title for it, Double Jack Stomp.
Was that in a movie or something? Did you ever make any movies?

I made a movie. Oh, I made a lot of movies. I was in Bella the 90s with Mae Weston. I was in Earl Carol Vanity, Murder at the Vanity. I was in Black and Tan Fantasy. I was in Backstage. I was... Was it a check and double check movie? That was Amos Nandy in 31. We made that with Amos Nandy. I guess that's how that... Yeah. Yeah. So, he got that title from Amos Nandy, Double Jack Stomp.
What was your very first record, by the way? Yeah.
My very first record were Bunyan Hand Breakdown and Black and Tan Fantasy.
You never did record with Elga? No.
None of those guys. No, none of those guys wasn't recording. We didn't have the opportunity to record. We had the right material, but... We just didn't have the opportunity to record at that time.
I've had another question. We'll keep mixing up all these questions and not in any...
See, Mamie Smith was the first colored artist to record. Yeah.
I wanted to ask about the seating of the band. How did they sit or stand? In which order?
Well, just whatever order that the studio would place.
I mean, in the old New Orleans bands when you first heard them.
The old New Orleans band, we set all up in a bunch right together.
I mean, was the bass on one end or in the back?

The bass is on the rhythm sections always together. The drums and the piano are always together. You know, if it was possible. Sometimes it wasn't possible. But wherever it was possible, it was just the same, because we could feel each other. They used much piano then? Well, we were using piano the whole time I played. I never played as much with guitar the song around here. Yeah, well, I mean down here... We used to use guitar instead of piano around here, you know what I mean? Because you had more of one night stands. The only place that they used piano was in the district. Fellas like Buddy Christian, he was a great district man.
Was he still in the New Orleans band?
Oh yeah, he had a gig band around here.
He was a 12 year.
Great guy. Still looked well too.
Did they ever use banjos when you were down here much?

No, guitar. Only after I left here, when banjos got popular, I think around 1917 or 18, because all the bands up north were using banjos. Did they use tubas in the band? And I had a friend of mine by the name of Wilbur Sweatman, I guess you heard that. He wrote the Down Home Rag. Where...
This is not that master, it's a different one. This is the Bluebird I got here.
That's the Bluebird. That's the Victor Bluebird. Bluebird label.
I think it was originally on Victor, I don't remember for sure.
Yeah, it's originally. That was the Bluebird label. Oh, French. Oh, French. Yeah. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. For more information visit www.fema.gov
